title: YAGNI Priniciple
summary: YAGNI means do not build for a future that has not arrived: implement the current requirement in the simplest form that passes, and pay for abstraction only when the second real use case forces it.

refs.title: YAGNI Principle in Software Development - GeeksforGeeks
Mastering Efficiency: Exploring the YAGNI Principle in Java Development

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: **Every speculative abstraction is a loan you pay interest on forever.** YAGNI says: build only what the current requirement demands. If you cannot point to a caller, a ticket, or a test that needs it *today*, delete it. Future flexibility is not free — it is carry cost.
What it is, precisely

YAGNI — You Aren't Gonna Need It — is a constraint on design scope: **do not implement behavior, extension points, or generality beyond what is required to satisfy the known, current use cases.** It is not laziness and it is not an excuse to write rigid code. It is a decision rule about *when* to generalize. You write clean, tested, refactorable code for what exists now, and you deliberately refuse to add parameters, frameworks, flags, or base classes for what *might* exist later. The reason is probabilistic: most predicted futures never happen, and the ones that do happen arrive in a different shape than you guessed.

The precise boundary matters because candidates blur it. YAGNI does **not** say avoid design. It says avoid *presumptive* design — code that supports a feature no user can invoke yet. Adding a `paymentMethod` enum with `CRYPTO` and `BANK_TRANSFER` when only `CARD` ships is a YAGNI violation. Extracting a method so the current logic is readable is not. Writing a test for the current path is not. Making a field `private` instead of `protected just in case someone subclasses` is YAGNI applied correctly. The test is simple: if you removed the speculative part, would any current test fail or any current caller break? If no, it should not exist.

items: **Current requirement only:** build the smallest behavior that satisfies a real caller today.
**No speculative generality:** no extra config knobs, no plugin interfaces for one plugin, no generic managers.
**Refactor on evidence:** when the second concrete use case arrives, *then* you extract the abstraction — with two examples to get the shape right.

blocks.text: The mechanism

YAGNI works because it replaces prediction with reaction. Prediction is expensive and usually wrong. Reaction is cheap *if* the code is kept simple and covered by tests. So the mechanism is a loop: implement minimally, keep coupling low, and let duplication or a second case trigger the generalization. You defer the abstraction decision until you have two real data points, which is the minimum needed to see what actually varies. The trade-off you are making is explicit: you accept a higher chance of localized rework later in exchange for lower complexity, fewer bugs, and faster delivery now.

blocks.title: YAGNI decision loop
blocks.caption: Build minimal now, generalize only on second evidence.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
    A[Proposed addition] --> B{Required by current use case?}
    B -->|No| C[Do not build]
    B -->|Yes| D[Build smallest version that works]
    D --> E{Second real use case appears?}
    E -->|No| F[Leave it alone]
    E -->|Yes| G[Refactor to abstraction]
    C --> H[Lower carry cost]
    F --> H
    G --> H

blocks.text: Why this order? Because the cost of a wrong abstraction dwarfs the cost of a late abstraction. A correct abstraction discovered from two cases takes an hour to extract. A wrong framework built upfront takes weeks to build, then months of workarounds when reality diverges. Teams that build the framework first end up with a generic system that fits neither the first nor the second case. Teams that wait end up with a concrete system that is easy to reshape. That is the core bet: **rework on simple code is cheaper than maintenance on speculative code.** The trade-off flips only when change is genuinely irreversible — a shipped file format, a public API contract, a data migration — and those are the exceptions, not the rule.
The trade-offs, honestly

blocks.caption: YAGNI is a bet on information arriving later. Price both sides.
rows: Ship faster; less code to test and review
Block future work waiting on unused scaffolding that may never be used
Less carry cost; every line you skip is a line you never debug
More paths, more flags, more interactions to reason about on every change
Abstractions fit reality because they are derived from two real cases
Abstractions guess wrong; you lock in the wrong seam and pay to work around it
Risk: you may rework a concrete implementation when case two arrives
Risk: you build for a future that never arrives, or arrives differently
Risk: painful if the decision is hard to reverse (schema, wire protocol)
Benefit: justified only when reversal cost exceeds carry cost and probability is high

blocks.text: How it fails in production

Speculative code does not fail loudly. It rots. The symptom is velocity collapse: a simple ticket — change the retry delay, add a field, rename a status — touches five layers, four flags, and a strategy factory with one real implementation and three stubs. On-call sees it differently: dead branches hide live bugs. A `if (mode == ADVANCED)` path that never shipped in production still compiles, still gets merged around, and breaks silently when a dependency upgrades because nothing exercises it. Coverage tools show the lie: the speculative module sits at 0% or fake 100% with mock-only tests. The other failure is subtler: the team stops deleting. Once a generic `AbstractProcessorFactoryRegistry` exists, nobody has the authority to remove it, so every new feature is bent to fit it. Complexity becomes load-bearing.

items: **Symptom: flag sprawl.** Config options nobody can explain, all set to defaults. Changing one breaks an untested combination.
**Symptom: single-implementation interfaces.** `PaymentStrategy` with exactly one class `CardPaymentStrategy` for eighteen months, plus a factory, plus a registry.
**Symptom: speculative error handling.** Retries, fallbacks, and sharding logic for scale you have never measured, masking the real bottleneck.
**Symptom: fear to delete.** Engineers route new logic through the old generic hook because removing the hook feels riskier than abusing it.

blocks.title: Carry cost is the killer
blocks.text: Building costs once. Carrying costs on every read, every merge, every debug session. A 200-line plugin framework for a single use case is not 200 lines — it is 200 lines times every engineer who must understand it before touching adjacent code. **Trade-off to state out loud:** you are trading one-time build savings now for compounding comprehension cost later, or vice versa.
Concrete example in code

This is the pattern interviewers probe for. The left design anticipates five payment types, a rule engine, and a config-driven registry. Only cards exist. The right design solves cards directly and leaves a clean seam for extraction later. The right design is not less engineered — it is engineered at the correct time.

Why the second version wins: it has one path to test, one failure mode, and no indirection to hold in your head. If a wallet payment arrives next quarter, you duplicate three lines, notice the shared shape, and extract an interface with real knowledge of what varies — gateway call, idempotency key, reconciliation — instead of guessing it. The objection is always what if extraction is painful? Answer directly: extraction from simple, tested code is mechanical. Maintenance of a wrong abstraction is not. Only invert this when the seam crosses a hard boundary you cannot refactor later, like a persisted column or a versioned network contract. Then you design the seam upfront and say why.
How it shows up in an interview
No interviewer asks define YAGNI and stops. They embed it in a design task and watch whether you gold-plate. Your job is to scope aggressively and narrate the trade-off as you cut.

items.title: Scope the MVP out loud
items.text: For a task like design a parking lot or a cache: state what you are NOT building. No multi-floor pricing engine, no distributed eviction, no admin analytics — until asked. This is graded.

items.title: Resist the framework reflex
items.text: When you feel the urge to add an abstract factory, a generic manager, or a config flag, pause and ask: is there a second caller in the requirements? If not, hardcode with a named constant and move on.

items.title: Name the reversal cost
items.text: Say: I am hardcoding this because changing it later is a five-line refactor. I would NOT hardcode the storage schema, because migrating stored data later is expensive. That sentence separates mid-level from senior.

items.title: Handle the extensibility follow-up
items.text: When pressed with what if we add X?, do not pre-build X. Sketch how you WOULD extract the seam: which class splits, where the interface goes, what breaks. Design for replaceability, not predicted reuse.

items.title: Delete on request
items.text: If the interviewer adds scope, add it. If they narrow scope, delete the now-dead generality immediately. Leaving dead abstraction after a scope cut is a fail signal.

blocks.text: Misconceptions that fail candidates

items: **YAGNI means no design.** Wrong. It means no *speculative* design. Low coupling, clear names, and tests are mandatory — they are what make late refactoring cheap.
**YAGNI means never think ahead.** Wrong. Think ahead, but do not *build* ahead. Noting where a seam would go is good judgment; coding the seam with one implementation is waste.

**YAGNI conflicts with SOLID.** Wrong. Open-closed and dependency inversion still apply — applied when variation is real, not imagined. An interface with one implementation created on day one is not SOLID, it is clutter.

**Copy-paste is always better than abstraction.** Wrong. Duplication of a stable, well-understood three lines twice is fine. Duplication of complex branching five times is not simplicity, it is negligence. The trigger for abstraction is the second or third real repetition.
**Prototypes are exempt.** Dangerous. Prototype code that ships becomes production code. If you cut corners under YAGNI, isolate the hack, mark the seam, and state the payback condition.

blocks.text: When to apply it and when to ignore it

YAGNI is the default, not a dogma. Override it only when two conditions hold together: the future need is high-probability *and* the cost of changing course later is disproportionate. A checklist beats intuition here.

blocks.caption: Default to YAGNI; break the rule only with evidence.
rows: Business logic with one known variant; second variant is a rumor
Wire protocol, file format, or public API where v1 mistakes persist for years
UI options, report types, notification channels not yet requested
Security, audit, or compliance hooks legally required before launch
Performance sharding, caching layers, or async pipelines before a measured bottleneck
Capacity or correctness constraint already proven by load data or a hard limit
Generic admin consoles, rule engines, or DSLs proposed to avoid future coding
Irreversible data model choice: tenant isolation, currency representation, time zones

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: **YAGNI means I implement only the current requirement in its simplest working form and defer generalization until a second real use case reveals the correct abstraction — trading possible localized rework later for guaranteed lower complexity now.**
